source: Zheng, Zhou, Meng, Zhou, Huang (2024) Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors (ICLR 2024)
finding: LLMs pick some option labels more than others. Moving the correct answer to a fixed slot changes accuracy a lot. Most of the bias is a prior for label tokens (A, B, C, D), not a pure position effect. Position bias is present but irregular.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks (MMLU, ARC, CSQA). MMLU 0-shot: gpt-3.5-turbo 67.2 original, 60.9 when the gold answer is always D (-6.3). llama-30B gains 15.2 when gold is always A. With gold balanced 250 each over 1,000 items, llama-30B picks A/B/C/D 34.6/27.3/22.3/15.8% of the time. Removing option IDs cut the recall spread (RStd) from 5.5 to 1.0 on gpt-3.5-turbo; CoT and debiasing instructions did not.
quote: moving the golden answers to position D degrades the accuracy of gpt-3.5-turbo by 6.3
limits: Models are 2023 vintage (llama-2, gpt-3.5, vicuna). 4 to 5 options only. Question answering with a known gold answer, not open candidate selection.
agent_relevance: Shuffle candidate order and label candidates by content or neutral IDs when the agent selects among candidates; cyclic permutation is the cheap baseline. Re-measure on current models.

source: Shi, Ma, Liang, Diao, Ma, Vosoughi (2024) Judging the Judges: A Systematic Study of Position Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: Position bias in LLM judges is real, not random, and varies by judge and task. It is weakly tied to prompt length but strongly tied to how close the candidates are in quality: the smaller the quality gap, the more the order decides.
numbers: 15 LLM judges, MTBench and DevBench, 22 tasks, about 40 solution-generating models, over 150,000 evaluation instances. Pairwise and list-wise (2 or 3 options). Metrics: repetition stability, position consistency, preference fairness.
limits: Read the abstract and method text; per-judge tables not extracted. Judges, not selectors that also generate. 2024 models.
agent_relevance: When two candidates are close, the order the agent sees them in matters most, and close calls are where selection matters. Randomise order and run a swapped re-check on near ties only.

source: Liu, Lin, Hewitt, Paranjape, Bevilacqua, Petroni, Liang (2023/2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: In multi-document QA, accuracy is highest when the relevant document is first or last and lowest in the middle (U-shaped). Adding more documents (10, 20, 30) lowers accuracy.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 closed-book 56.1%, oracle (only the gold document) 88.3%. With 20 documents, performance can drop by more than 20% in the worst gold position, sometimes below closed-book.
limits: 2023 models, retrieval QA, not candidate selection. Later long-context models may have narrowed the effect (not tested here).
agent_relevance: First-seen and last-seen items get an advantage in a long candidate list. Keep the list short and randomise order. Also a measured cost of larger set sizes (10 to 30 documents) for an LLM reader.

source: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder, Todd (2010) Can there ever be too many options? A meta-analytic review of choice overload (J Consumer Research)
finding: Across 63 conditions in 50 experiments the mean effect of a large assortment is about zero, with large unexplained spread. Prior preferences or expertise protect against overload. Published studies show more overload than unpublished. No linear relation with the size of the large set.
numbers: N=5,036. Mean D = 0.02, 95% CI about -0.09 to 0.12 (minus signs lost in the PDF text; sign inferred from the CI midpoint). tau-squared 0.12 (CI 0.08 to 0.25), Q(62)=192, p<.001, I-squared 68%. After 20% trimming D = 0.001 and I-squared 22%. Meta-regression explains 56% of the variance: prior preferences/expertise b=.50, published vs unpublished b=.27, consumption outcome b=.87 (more choice better). The introduction recounts the jam study (24 vs 6 jams) and a plan-participation result where 48% took part in the small-assortment condition (large-condition figure not read).
quote: a mean effect size of virtually zero but considerable variance between studies
limits: Human consumer choices, mostly low-stakes products. Seven studies reporting only 'ns' were coded as zero. Not a test on LLMs.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a larger candidate list hurts an LLM selector. The effect depends on set complexity, task difficulty, and whether the chooser has a clear target. Run the 3/6/12/24 test rather than copy a rule.

source: Chernev, Boeckenholt, Goodman (2015) Choice overload: A conceptual review and meta-analysis (J Consumer Psychology)
finding: Re-analysis finds that large assortments do raise choice overload once four moderators are included: set complexity, decision task difficulty, preference uncertainty and an effort-minimizing goal. Satisfaction/confidence, regret, deferral and switching are about equally good outcome measures.
numbers: 99 observations, N=7,202. The abstract gives no mean d or CI; the full text is paywalled (Crossref abstract only).
limits: Abstract only. Numeric overall d with CI not obtained. The two meta-analyses disagree on the overall effect, partly through study selection and moderator coding.
agent_relevance: The four moderators map onto agent cases: many similar candidates, hard discrimination, unclear criterion, low effort budget. They are what to vary in a set-size test.

source: Damani, Shenfeld, Peng, Bobu, Andreas (2024) Learning How Hard to Think: Input-Adaptive Allocation of LM Computation
finding: A small learned predictor on the query's hidden states can predict how much extra samples will help. Using it to set best-of-k size or to route to a stronger decoder saves compute at the same reward. A reward model or verifier is still needed to pick the final answer.
numbers: Same reward with up to 50% less compute on Math and Code; Chat 0 to 10% (full set), 25 to 40% on the high/low-variance tranche subset. Routing calls the expensive decoder only 50 to 75% of the time. Predictor, median-split accuracy: Code 74%, Math 84%, Chat routing 72%; loss 0.33 (Code) and 0.48 (Math) vs fixed baselines 0.58 and 0.69. About 50% of Code problems have zero success rate; Math 5%.
limits: Needs training data per domain and a reward model. Impossible items (0% success) are a trap: a wrong forecast gives them a large budget. Gemma-2B/7B scale, Llama-3 reward model; not frontier models.
agent_relevance: A cheap difficulty probe is learnable from the query alone, and 72 to 84% accuracy on easy-vs-hard ranking is the realistic ceiling. Keep a floor of one extra pass for low-confidence cases because 16 to 28% are mis-ranked.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Stop sampling when the answer votes agree (consensus >= 0.95) and drop low-confidence traces early using token-probability confidence. No answer key is needed. Compared with majority voting at a fixed 512-trace budget it uses 18 to 85% fewer tokens, with accuracy mostly kept and sometimes higher.
numbers: Budget K=512, warm-up 16 traces. DeepConf-low vs cons@512 token cut 43 to 79% (text), DeepConf-high 18 to 59%. DeepSeek-8B AIME24 86.7 to 92.5% at -77.9% tokens. GPT-OSS-120B AIME25 97.1 to 97.9% at -84.7%. A few cells lose accuracy: Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9; GPT-OSS-120B HMMT25 92.8 to 92.0 at -76.2%. Offline GPT-OSS-120B AIME25 99.9% vs 97.0 cons@512 vs 91.8 pass@1.
quote: it can sometimes hurt performance due to model overconfidence on incorrect problems
limits: Baseline is a fixed 512-trace vote, not an equal-token baseline; tokens and accuracy are both reported, so it is a Pareto comparison. Competition math only (AIME24/25, BRUMO25, HMMT25). Authors note overconfidence on wrong problems (GPT-OSS-120B), so aggressive filtering (top 10%) can hurt. All samples come from one model, so agreement is correlated (G4).
agent_relevance: Strongest published support that a label-free stop (consensus threshold plus confidence) beats a fixed budget. Use the conservative setting (keep 90%) when errors are costly.

source: Li, Yuan, Feng, Pan, Wang, Sun, Wang, Li (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency for Multi-step Reasoning (ICLR 2024)
finding: Sample in small windows (size 5) and stop when all answers in a window agree. This is a label-free first-agreement stop. It cuts the number of samples a lot with comparable accuracy.
numbers: Sample reduction: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%, vs sampling to a preset size. The saving is largest on easy sets and smallest on MATH, so it is difficulty-sensitive by design. Predicted vs actual cost for the control scheme correlates above 0.8 (Pearson).
limits: Counts samples, not tokens. Older models (GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 class). Within-window agreement assumes independent draws; correlated errors make a unanimous window wrong.
agent_relevance: A window-agreement stop is simple to implement and fits S0: easy items stop after one window, hard ones keep sampling.

source: Liu, Wang (2025) Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
finding: Reasoning models often reach their final answer well before they stop thinking. How early depends on the task: open QA converges almost at once, math late. Label-free stops (answer consistency across chunks, a think-token tweak) work on easy tasks but are unstable on harder ones; a supervised learned stop is more robust.
numbers: Answer-convergence ratio peaks near 0.0 on NaturalQuestions, about 0.8 on GSM8K and MATH-500, about 0.9 on GPQA and AIME24. Five open models (R1-Qwen 7B/32B, R1-Llama 8B/70B, QwQ-32B), five benchmarks. Abstract: Answer Consistency cuts NaturalQuestions tokens by over 40% while accuracy rises. Learn-to-Stop cuts NQ tokens 46.2% (R1-Qwen-7B), 47.7% (R1-Qwen-32B), 34.1% and 46.4% on the Llama models. Models typically converge after about 60% of the reasoning steps on math.
limits: Table cells were scrambled in text extraction; only text claims used. R1-distilled models, mid-2025. Greedy decoding for the convergence analysis.
agent_relevance: First direct non-math check of Chen's 'answer is there early' finding (open QA): the effect is bigger on easy QA. Hard sets need a supervised or verifier signal, as K06 predicts.

source: Yang, Si, Duan, Zhu, Zhu, Li, Chen, Lin, Wang (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: At step transitions the model gives a trial answer; if its confidence is high, thinking stops. Training-free. Works on math, science QA and code across 11 reasoning models.
numbers: 10 benchmarks, 11 models: chain length -19.1% to -80.1%, accuracy +0.3 to +5.0 points (abstract). Code, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B: HumanEval 91.5 to 93.9 at 3,861 to 1,254 tokens; LiveCodeBench 56.0 to 56.6 at 9,109 to 3,677; BigCodeBench 44.5 to 46.1. Qwen3-14B LiveCodeBench 73.4 to 74.1 at 66.3% of tokens.
limits: Baseline is the full chain of thought, not an equal-token or best-of-N baseline. Trial answers add latency in code. PUMA (d12) reports DEER gives inconsistent efficiency.
agent_relevance: Yes for code: a label-free confidence stop kept pass@1 on three code benchmarks with 34 to 80% of the tokens. Partly answers gap 7 outside math.

source: Zhang, Chen, Pan, Zhao, Panda, Li, He (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: A small probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct (ROC-AUC above 0.7, ECE below 0.1 in distribution). Thresholding the probe score as an early-exit rule cut tokens by up to 24% without losing accuracy. Calibration falls out of distribution.
numbers: R1-Distill-Llama-8B and others: ECE < 0.1, ROC-AUC > 0.7 in distribution; early exit up to -24% tokens at equal accuracy. Probes trained on MATH and GSM8K transfer to each other but are less calibrated on AIME; they do not transfer from logical reasoning to math. ECE minimum 0.03 late in the chain.
limits: Needs trained probes and open weights. Calibration measured per dataset and within one chain, not under correlated resampling, so gap 9 is only partly answered.
agent_relevance: A calibrated stop signal is possible but domain-specific. Re-calibrate per task type before trusting a threshold.

source: Min, Vaccarino, Chen, Wu, Yona, Cheng (2026) Stop When Reasoning Converges: Semantic-Preserving Early Exit for Reasoning Models (PUMA)
finding: Answer-level stop signals (confidence, trial-answer consistency) often fire too early. A large share of their failures are cases where the full chain would have corrected itself. Adding a redundancy detector plus answer verification gives a safer stop.
numbers: Five reasoning models, five benchmarks. Counterfactual test: 42.4% of confidence-based stop failures and 54.8% of consistency-based failures are premature (the full chain ends correct). PUMA: 26.2% average token reduction, accuracy kept; LiveCodeBench 18 to 19% fewer tokens, at most 1.5 points pass@1 change. Prompt-brevity baselines on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking fall to 54.3 / 45.3 / 59.6% vs 81.7% for Full CoT; Answer Convergence stops aggressively with severe accuracy collapse.
limits: May 2026 preprint, not peer reviewed. Table 7 row values scrambled in extraction; text figures used. Gain is smaller than DeepConf or DEER because the design is conservative.
agent_relevance: Measured cost of a wrong or too-eager stop signal on hard items (gaps 2 and 9): about half of the failures are recoverable. Require a verifier or redundancy check before an early stop on hard items.

source: Tan, He, Liu, Zhao (2025) The Zero-Step Thinking: An Empirical Study of Mode Selection as Harder Early Exit in Reasoning Models
finding: Deciding at the start (think or no-think) is harder than deciding midway. Nine baselines tested. Prompt-based selection often fails; methods using internal states do better but are unstable across datasets and models.
numbers: Datasets GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME25, GPQA-Diamond. Best single case: ProbeConf ROC-AUC 72.2 on AIME25 with a 1.5B model; the advantage did not carry to the 7B model or other datasets. Best Brier 0.181 on AIME25. No single method won everywhere.
limits: Small distilled models (1.5B, 7B). Zero-step means no reasoning has been done yet.
agent_relevance: A zero-cost difficulty gate at S0 from the question alone is unreliable. Prefer a probe that uses a first partial attempt or a pilot sample.

source: Hassid, Synnaeve, Adi, Schwartz (2025/2026) Don't Overthink it: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: For the same question, shorter reasoning chains are more often right. Running k chains in parallel and stopping at the first m to finish (short-m@k) with a majority vote beats plain majority voting at lower cost.
numbers: Shorter chains up to 34.5% more accurate than the longest chain for the same question. short-1@k: same or better than majority vote in low-compute settings with up to 40% fewer thinking tokens. short-3@k: beats majority voting across budgets with up to 33% wall-time reduction. Models include LN-Super-49B and R1-32B on GPQA-D, AIME24/25, HMMT.
limits: Math and science QA only (abstract and setup read). Finishing early is a proxy for easy and confident, not an answer key; it can fail on items that need long chains.
agent_relevance: A label-free first-finished rule is a satisficing stop that needs only the sample lengths. Test it as a cheap S0 alternative.

source: Chehade et al. (2025) Bounded Rationality for LLMs: Satisficing Alignment at Inference-Time (re-check of baselines and judges)
finding: Re-read for gap 10. Experiments compare against decoding baselines (ARGS-style and multi-objective decoding) and use GPT-4 win-tie rates. Best-of-K appears in related work but is not an experimental arm. No human raters are reported. The threshold plot shows the target-reward win rate flattens at higher thresholds.
numbers: About +10% win-tie in one summary line and +22.3% for helpfulness in the abstract (previously confirmed). The threshold sweep shows a plateau, read by the authors as 'a threshold suffices'.
limits: GPT-4 judge only; no human judges; no equal-sample best-of-N arm; 7B models. Gap 10 is NOT closed by this paper.
agent_relevance: Treat as proof of concept. If we use threshold-constrained selection, add best-of-N at equal samples as the control.

source: Artinger, Gigerenzer, Jacobs (2022) Satisficing: Integrating Two Traditions (J Economic Literature)
finding: Under risk (known probabilities) satisficing is usually inferior to optimising and is modelled inside the neoclassical frame. Under uncertainty satisficing strategies are often derived from data and can be highly effective. The review gives conditions where satisficing is rational.
numbers: Survey of more than 60 years across economics, psychology and management. No new numbers read.
quote: under uncertainty, satisficing strategies are often derived empirically and can be highly effective
limits: Abstract only (Crossref); the open post-print on pure.mpg.de returned 403, so the conditions list was not read. No LLM tasks reviewed.
agent_relevance: Classify tasks as risk-like (checkable, known success rate, e.g. unit-test code) or uncertain (open-ended, no answer key). Optimise/verify in the first, use simple stops in the second. This split is untested for LLM agents.

source: Secretary problem: optimal 37% rule and human experiments (Seale and Rapoport 1997; Bearden, Rapoport and Murphy 2006; via Wikipedia secondary text)
finding: The optimal rule rejects the first n/e (about 37%) and then takes the first better-than-all-so-far; the best option is chosen about 36.8% of the time. The page says people tend to stop searching too soon, without magnitudes.
numbers: 1/e = 0.368. No human numbers on the page. Seale and Rapoport (10.1006/obhd.1997.2683) and Bearden et al. (10.1002/bdm.521) exist in Crossref but are paywalled; abstracts not available.
limits: Secondary source; the page flags its section as single-source. Simon 1955/1956 and Todd and Miller 1999 could not be opened: Nobel PDF 403, JSTOR not served, Sage mirror 403.
agent_relevance: Assume our agent's stop timing is also biased and measure it; the human 'stop early' direction is not proof for LLMs.

source: Negative search result: adaptive aspiration levels in LLM agents, and candidate-set-size studies for LLM selectors (2024 to 2026)
finding: arXiv title and abstract searches found no paper on adaptive aspiration (raise after success, lower after failure) for LLM agents, and no LLM choice-overload paper varying candidate-set size. Hits were planning, bandit and robust-optimisation papers plus Chehade 2025. WebSearch quota ran out and Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and later arXiv queries returned 429, so coverage is partial.
numbers: ti:satisficing: 10 results, none on LLM aspiration. abs:aspiration AND LLM AND agents: 8 results, none relevant. satisficing AND LLM: 7 results, only Chehade 2025 and a 2026 analysis of LLM optimality on planning (2604.02910) related. Choice-overload-in-LLM queries failed with rate limits.
limits: Absence of evidence from a rate-limited search, not proof of absence. Nearby: Damani 2024 adapts compute to difficulty (d06) but not an aspiration level; DeepConf sets its filter threshold from a warm-up (d07).
agent_relevance: Adaptive aspiration is an untested idea for our agent: raise the pass threshold after clean passes and lower it after repeated near-misses, compared at equal tokens.

source: Synthesis of d01 to d03: order effects in LLM selection (answer to gap 4)
finding: Three independent LLM studies show order effects: a label-token prior, a first or last advantage, and a U-shape across 20 documents. So yes, order matters for LLMs, though the cause is mostly a label prior in Zheng and context position in Liu. The effect grows when candidates are close in quality (Shi).
numbers: d01: 6.3 point accuracy loss at slot D (gpt-3.5); d03: more than 20% worst-case drop with 20 documents; d02: effect tied to quality gap across 150,000 instances.
limits: All three use 2023 to 2024 models. No 2025 to 2026 frontier-model position-bias measurement was opened here.
agent_relevance: Order-randomise and compare; log the position of the chosen candidate to detect residual first-seen bias.
